clinicalPearls: The most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, usually diagnosed before 5 years of age.
Leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex, sometimes first noticed in photographs) is the most common presenting sign and warrants urgent ophthalmology referral.
Strabismus is the second most common presentation and should never be dismissed without excluding an intraocular cause.
Disease may be unilateral or bilateral; bilateral and multifocal tumours are almost always heritable.
Heritable retinoblastoma arises from germline mutation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene and carries a lifelong risk of second malignancies, especially osteosarcoma.
Diagnosis is made clinically by an experienced ophthalmologist under examination, supported by imaging; biopsy is avoided because of the risk of tumour seeding.
Treatment aims to save life first, then preserve the eye and vision, using approaches such as chemotherapy, focal therapies, and enucleation for advanced disease.
Children with heritable disease and affected families need genetic counselling and long-term surveillance for new tumours and secondary cancers.
reference.pathophysiology: Retinoblastoma results from biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene in developing retinal cells. In heritable disease one mutated allele is inherited or arises in the germline, and a second somatic hit inactivates the remaining allele, producing early, often bilateral, multifocal tumours (consistent with the two-hit hypothesis). Loss of functional RB protein removes control of the cell cycle at the G1-S checkpoint, driving unregulated proliferation of retinal precursor cells and tumour formation.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous)
Endophthalmitis or other causes of leukocoria
additionalInvestigations: Detailed dilated fundus examination under anaesthesia by an ocular oncology team
Ocular ultrasound and MRI of the orbits and brain
RB1 genetic testing and genetic counselling
Examination of the fellow eye and screening of at-risk relatives
Evaluation for metastatic or trilateral (pineal) disease when clinically indicated
redFlags: Leukocoria in any child requires urgent same-pathway ophthalmology referral to exclude retinoblastoma
New-onset strabismus without an obvious benign cause
Rapidly progressive proptosis or an inflamed, painful eye suggesting advanced or extraocular spread
Bilateral disease or a family history indicating heritable retinoblastoma
Signs of intracranial (trilateral) disease such as neurological deterioration
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and modern therapy, survival in high-resource settings exceeds 95 percent for intraocular disease; extraocular or metastatic spread markedly worsens outcome. Children with heritable disease remain at elevated lifelong risk of second malignancies.
pitfalls: Dismissing leukocoria or a subtle white reflex noticed in photographs as artefact
Attributing strabismus solely to a benign squint without a dilated fundus examination
Delaying urgent referral, which can be the difference between saving and losing an eye or life
Overlooking the need for genetic testing and family screening in apparently unilateral disease
management: Tailor treatment to laterality and stage, using focal therapy with laser or transpupillary thermotherapy, cryotherapy or plaque brachytherapy for small tumours
Use chemoreduction with systemic or intra-arterial ophthalmic-artery chemotherapy, adding intravitreal chemotherapy for vitreous seeding, to preserve the eye where possible
Perform enucleation for advanced unilateral disease not amenable to eye-preserving therapy, and avoid biopsy because of the risk of tumour seeding
Reserve external beam radiotherapy for selected cases given the heightened second-malignancy risk in heritable disease
Give adjuvant chemotherapy for high-risk histology or extraocular and metastatic spread
Undertake RB1 genetic testing with counselling and screening of at-risk relatives and the fellow eye
Manage through a specialist ocular oncology multidisciplinary team and maintain lifelong surveillance for second malignancies such as osteosarcoma
